entities.name: Martín de Zalba
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Martín de Zalba (died 1403) emerged as a pivotal Navarrese cleric and statesman during the tumultuous late 14th century, a period defined by the Hundred Years' War and the profound rupture of the Western Schism. Serving as the chancellor of the Kingdom of Navarre from 1376 to 1396 and concurrently as the bishop of Pamplona from 1377 until his death, Zalba was a towering figure in both secular administration and ecclesiastical affairs. His elevation to cardinal by Antipope Clement VII in 1390 solidified his significance, making him a key player in the Avignon obedience and a crucial diplomatic asset for Navarre amidst the complex political landscape of medieval Iberia and Europe.

His chancellorship under King Charles II and later Charles III was marked by astute diplomacy and administrative competence. Zalba was instrumental in navigating Navarre's precarious position between the powerful kingdoms of France and Castile, consistently working to preserve the kingdom's independence and territorial integrity. As bishop of Pamplona, he oversaw significant church reforms and maintained the ecclesiastical infrastructure, while his cardinalate involved him directly in the high-stakes efforts to heal the papal schism, participating in councils and negotiations aimed at unifying the Church.

Zalba's dual role as a high-ranking cleric and a supreme secular administrator ensured that his influence rippled through both the temporal and spiritual domains of Navarre. His diplomatic efforts contributed significantly to the kingdom's stability during a period of widespread conflict, securing its borders and fostering economic relations. Furthermore, his steadfast loyalty to the Avignon Papacy, even amidst growing calls for a unified papacy, provided vital support for Clement VII's cause in the Iberian Peninsula, influencing the allegiances of other regional powers.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Martín de Zalba's dual role as chancellor of Navarre and cardinal of the Avignon Papacy significantly influenced Navarrese foreign policy and provided crucial support for one side of the Western Schism, impacting regional politics and religious allegiances during a tumultuous era.
